271: The three-factor interaction was non-significant. Among the thirty six treatment combinations, the maximum value of 25.16 mg QE/100 g was recorded by Kalojira grown at Birbhum/Howrah and sampled as fresh paddy, and the minimum of 6.52 mg QE/100 g by Gobindabhog grown at Purba Bardhaman and sampled at 12 months. Given the non-significance of this term, these two extreme cells cannot be interpreted as genuine differences in isolation, and the main effects afford the more reliable inference.
278: Flavonoids constitute one family within the phenolic group and account for much of the antioxidant activity of pigmented grain, so that their conformity to the same varietal and locational ranking as total phenol is unsurprising. They declined more slowly during storage, and the most probable reason is chemical stability: many grain flavonoids carry attached sugar moieties, and glycosylation affords protection against the oxidation that degrades simple phenolic acids more readily. That none of the interactions attained significance for this trait, in contrast to total phenol and antioxidant capacity, indicates a straightforward first-order breakdown governed by time and ambient conditions rather than by genotype or growing site. The consistently higher values of the pigmented landrace accord with Zhang et al. (2010) and Shao et al. (2014), who demonstrated the flavonoid and anthocyanin load of coloured rice to reside principally in the outer layers of the grain.
282: Location exerted a highly significant effect on antioxidant capacity. The highest value, 41.35 mg TE/100 g, was recorded at Birbhum/Howrah, followed by Nadia with 34.83 mg TE/100 g and Purba Bardhaman with 28.73 mg TE/100 g. All three locations occupied separate letter groups, each differing significantly from the other two, and the extremes were separated by 12.62 mg TE/100 g.
284: The three landraces likewise differed, the varietal effect being highly significant. Kalojira recorded the highest value, 40.26 mg TE/100 g, followed by Radhunipagal with 34.74 mg TE/100 g and Gobindabhog with 29.91 mg TE/100 g. Each landrace occupied a discrete letter group, Kalojira exceeding Gobindabhog by 10.34 mg TE/100 g.
286: Storage period altered antioxidant capacity to a highly significant degree. In order of sampling, the values were 53.44 mg TE/100 g in fresh paddy, 38.95 mg TE/100 g at 4 months, 27.57 mg TE/100 g at 8 months and 19.92 mg TE/100 g at 12 months, the maximum occurring in fresh paddy and the minimum at 12 months. Over the full year the value declined by 62.7%.
288: The interaction between location and variety was highly significant. Kalojira at Birbhum/Howrah constituted the superior combination with 45.63 mg TE/100 g, and Gobindabhog at Purba Bardhaman the inferior one with 24.69 mg TE/100 g. The varietal sequence Kalojira, Radhunipagal, Gobindabhog was maintained at every location; the interaction therefore modified the magnitude of the varietal differences rather than their direction.
289: The interaction between location and storage was highly significant. The highest mean, 62.11 mg TE/100 g, was recorded for Birbhum/Howrah in fresh paddy and the lowest, 13.57 mg TE/100 g, for Purba Bardhaman at 12 months. Between fresh paddy and 12 months of storage the change amounted to -61.2% at Nadia, -70.4% at Purba Bardhaman and -58.3% at Birbhum/Howrah, a spread of 12.1 percentage points, grain from Purba Bardhaman changing most and that from Birbhum/Howrah least. The rate of change during storage was therefore not uniform across the three locations.
290: The interaction between variety and storage was highly significant. The highest mean, 61.13 mg TE/100 g, was recorded for Kalojira in fresh paddy and the lowest, 16.26 mg TE/100 g, for Gobindabhog at 12 months. Over the twelve months the change amounted to -63.8% in Gobindabhog, -64.6% in Radhunipagal and -60.2% in Kalojira, Radhunipagal shifting furthest and Kalojira least. The three landraces consequently did not gain or lose at equivalent rates during storage.
291: The three-factor interaction was highly significant. Among the thirty six treatment combinations, the maximum value of 69.63 mg TE/100 g was recorded by Kalojira grown at Birbhum/Howrah and sampled as fresh paddy, and the minimum of 10.42 mg TE/100 g by Gobindabhog grown at Purba Bardhaman and sampled at 12 months, a spread of 59.21 mg TE/100 g. This range is appreciably wider than that generated by any single factor in isolation. Location, landrace and storage period operated jointly, and the optimum result is obtainable only by setting all three at the appropriate level.
298: Antioxidant capacity expresses in a single figure the combined effect of all the protective compounds of the grain, and it declined more steeply during storage than any other trait determined. The salient point is that it declined faster than either total phenol or total flavonoid, so that phenolic loss alone cannot account for it. The most probable explanation is the concurrent loss of the lipid-associated antioxidants: tocopherols, tocotrienols and gamma-oryzanol are carried with the oil of the grain and are degraded as that oil is hydrolysed and oxidised, and the parallel decline of fat in this study supports that interpretation. Zhou et al. (2015) characterised these lipid, protein and starch changes as components of one connected ageing process rather than as separate events. The varietal and locational rankings corresponded to those for phenolics, which is to be expected given the close association between phenolic content and radical-scavenging activity in rice reported by Shao et al. (2014) and Zhou et al. (2004). Read alongside the aroma results, these findings define the useful storage life of these landraces: where they are valued for fragrance and for health-promoting compounds rather than for milling outturn alone, protracted ambient storage exacts a substantial and irrecoverable cost.

Gobindabhog at Birbhum/Howrah constituted the superior combination with 460.67 mg/100 g, and Kalojira at Birbhum/Howrah the inferior one with 175.02 mg/100 g. The ranking of the landraces was not conserved across locations: at Nadia the order was Gobindabhog, Kalojira, Radhunipagal; at Purba Bardhaman, Radhunipagal, Gobindabhog, Kalojira; and at Birbhum/Howrah, Gobindabhog, Radhunipagal, Kalojira. Rank reversal of this kind establishes that the landraces did not respond uniformly to the three growing environments.

Between fresh paddy and 12 months of storage the change amounted to -49.9% at Nadia, -36.8% at Purba Bardhaman and -35.8% at Birbhum/Howrah. The three locations changed by closely comparable margins, storage having acted upon the grain in much the same manner irrespective of where it was grown.

This range is appreciably wider than that generated by any single factor in isolation. 320: Phytic acid constitutes the phosphorus reserve of the seed and, at the same time, the principal anti-nutrient of cereal grain, since it chelates iron and zinc and precludes their absorption in the human gut. Its decline during storage is among the few changes recorded in this experiment that improve nutritional value, and the most probable basis is enzymatic. Endogenous phytase progressively removes phosphate groups from the phytic acid molecule, and the partially dephosphorylated forms bind minerals far less tightly (Fukushima et al., 2020). Rice carries less phytase than rye or wheat, yet sufficient to effect measurable hydrolysis where grain is held for months at ambient temperature and at the moisture levels prevailing here. The value of this becomes apparent only when read against the mineral results, which registered no change during storage: as phytate declines while minerals remain constant, the ratio between them improves, and a greater proportion of the iron and zinc of aged grain should be available to the body. The varietal differences are genotypic, grain phytic acid being a quantitative trait under polygenic control with useful natural variation among rice types, which permits selection for reduced phytate without recourse to induced mutants and the attendant penalties in germination and yield (Perera et al., 2018). The effect of growing site most probably follows the phosphorus status of the soil.
